sources.title: AI That Works #49: Prompt Injections & Guardrails
sources.note: Full transcript, README and meta read. Mostly Vaibhav demoing structured-output defences; Dex contributes the lethal trifecta, HumanLayer triage queue, layered guardrail tiers, defence in depth.

sources.title: AI That Works #50: MCP is Dead?
sources.note: Full transcript, README and meta read. Dex argues MCP is for user-brought tools, instruction budget, tool search critique, jagged frontier, signed per-action approval.

sources.title: AI That Works #51: No Vibes Allowed March Edition
sources.note: Full transcript, README and meta read. Vaibhav drives the BAML testing design session; Dex contributes context-window handling, doc-as-truth, dumb zone numbers, sycophancy and verifier points, WIP/bottleneck, CLAUDE.md conditional blocks.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We could have run cursor in a network sandbox
cards.claim: Dex frames prompt-injection risk as Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (untrusted content, private data, external communication) and says removing any one leg (cut prod DB access, network-sandbox to the inference API only, or put a guardrail) fixes it.
cards.evidence_detail: Walks through a disclosed Zendesk-to-Cursor-MCP exfiltration to a Supabase prod DB; no numbers.
cards.landing: Agent permission model for fixflow: no single agent session should hold untrusted input (customer text), prod DB credentials and outbound network together; relevant to WhatsApp dispatcher and any prod-DB-reading agent.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every issue gets reviewed by a human before it's allowed to be seen
cards.claim: HumanLayer puts a human triage queue between public GitHub issues and the Linear tickets its background agent can read, so outsiders cannot prompt-inject the agent or steer product work.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes HumanLayer's own practice; no incident or numbers.
cards.landing: Phase routine / ship plan: a human-gated intake before any agent reads externally authored text (issues, customer messages, scraped docs).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if the output contains any strings that were in the system message, block it
cards.claim: Dex names three guardrail tiers (deterministic rules on output, inference on the input before the main call, background inference) and says the cheap deterministic tier should go first, including substring-matching the system prompt in outputs.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual; ties to the earlier evals episode's deterministic tier.
cards.landing: Output backpressure: deterministic checks (grep/regex/CI contracts) before any LLM verifier; supports capped outputs and cheap scripts running before refuters.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you like kick off a background task, right?
cards.claim: Dex restates Vaibhav's design of a background guardrail agent that is launched on every new message added to the context and cancels the main stream if it flags a problem, rather than blocking in a linear pipeline.
cards.evidence_detail: Design sketch on whiteboard; Dex links it to an earlier voice-agent supervisor episode; Vaibhav adds a distilled sub-10ms classifier (OpenAI paper claimed, not shown).
cards.landing: A background supervisor/checker running alongside a phase session (e.g. watching for routine steps skipped) rather than a closing-message self-report; hooks-adjacent, re-opens skipped 'hooks' idea.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: layers of defense in depth so that even if someone pops one of them
cards.claim: Dex argues a single guardrail is never enough: stack string-contains, regex, structured-output validation, a light classifier and slower background classifiers, like infrastructure security layers.
cards.evidence_detail: Analogy to firewall/2FA/SSO/air-gap; no measurements.
cards.landing: Verifier design: layered cheap-to-expensive checks (lint, import-linter, tests, then Opus reviewer) with each layer having a named purpose.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have to be careful on the autonomy versus safety pipeline
cards.claim: Dex warns that each guardrail narrows what the agent can do (a guardrail that only allows event content makes everything about events) and that safety, speed and correctness must be balanced without hampering the agent.
cards.evidence_detail: Concerns false positives and latency; Vaibhav notes Claude Code/Codex default to broad permissions for this reason.
cards.landing: Guardrail/verifier tuning: refute-by-default verifiers have a false-positive cost; consider where strictness stops paying.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Never run the client of your inference on someone else's workstation.
cards.claim: Dex says anything running inference on the user's machine can be sniffed, so the system prompt is not a secret there; keep valuable prompts behind a cloud API.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites how Claude Code's system prompt was obtained via proxy; no numbers.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; FixFlow prompts are not IP. Possible relevance to what goes into the mobile app vs backend.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the instruction following for the system message will be stronger
cards.claim: Dex observes that instruction following for the system message is stronger than between user messages, which is why developer rules belong in the system role.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed in a live demo where a secret leaked from a user-role message but not a system-role one.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md placement: always-loaded system-level rules carry more weight than rules buried in chat or files read later.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: AI engineering is 90 % software engineering.
cards.claim: Dex endorses the view (via swyx) that AI engineering is mostly ordinary software engineering, so layering, caching and defence-in-depth patterns carry over directly.
cards.evidence_detail: Passing remark about a Twitter conversation.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; framing for treating the harness as ordinary engineering with tests and gates.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the best way to really learn how to do this stuff
cards.claim: Dex says the best way to learn these systems is to play with the models directly and watch the whole context window, as in the live prompt-injection iteration.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside during the demo.
cards.landing: Phase routine: hands-on trial runs (P1 cold-resume) are the way to learn what the routine does, not reading about it.

cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: MCP does not cause context rot.
cards.claim: Dex relays Kyle's point that the protocol is not what rots context; the design of the tools (tokens used, inefficient prompts) is, and the same tools as CLIs would rot it equally.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributed to his co-founder Kyle; no measurement given in this episode.
cards.landing: Skills/tools authoring: judge each tool or skill by the tokens and instructions it adds, not by its transport.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: MCP is not for a different way to call APIs.
cards.claim: Dex argues MCP is a plugin system for letting users bring tools you did not anticipate; if you know the functionality you need, write against the SDK instead.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument, with Claude Code extensibility as example.
cards.landing: Skill/agent design: build first-class, in-repo scripts for known needs; reserve external plugins for the long tail.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have an instruction budget for every model
cards.claim: Dex states every model has an instruction budget: the more instructions (including every function definition in an MCP server), the worse it adheres to any one, including the latest user message.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as established; Vaibhav cites GitHub MCP at ~50-60k tokens added per call.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim (W1): supports treating each rule line as spending a finite budget; also skill descriptions loaded every session.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Migrate it and build a first-class integration.
cards.claim: Dex's rule: do context engineering and token pinching on the high-use paths, let the long tail run through generic lower-quality mechanisms, and promote a long-tail item when usage shows it is popular.
cards.evidence_detail: Compares to the earlier reasoning episode: make it work on a beefy reasoning model, then optimise the frequent case for a small model.
cards.landing: Workflow library (W5) and effort routing (L1): save and tune only the workflows that recur; run rare ones generically at high effort.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: give people ways to visualize it
cards.claim: Dex praises Claude Code's /context command and says a harness should show users how many tokens MCPs and skills consume, then give tools to prune them (and tell users when an MCP has gone unused).
cards.evidence_detail: Refers to the Claude Code /context command; the unused-MCP warning is Vaibhav's idea that Dex likes.
cards.landing: Context-budget measurement: run /context at session start to record what CLAUDE.md, skills and agents cost; supports the W1 trim decision with a number.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Just remove the directory as a parameter
cards.claim: Dex says parameters the deterministic side already knows (e.g. the working directory) should be injected by a closure and removed from the tool schema so the model never has to pass them, and the tool schema should shrink to what the user has connected.
cards.evidence_detail: Code sketch of a ticket-fetch tool with zero/one/many sources; Vaibhav adds auditing highly frequent tools' parameters.
cards.landing: Custom agents/skills: scripts that take fewer arguments because the harness fills ids (shop, phase, SHA) itself.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the things that are super, super common should be here
cards.claim: Dex criticises Claude Code's tool-search design: the commonly used tools (read, edit, bash, fetch) should stay in the main context and only the rare ones be offloaded behind search, because making the agent search for the right tool adds turns.
cards.evidence_detail: Says he has seen the agent search to find a tool and the skill tool; Vaibhav agrees but states he could not share Codex details.
cards.landing: Skill loading: keep the few always-needed skills/rules always loaded, put rarely used material behind on-demand lookup.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If you are willing to put in the time and do this context engineering.
cards.claim: Dex argues models have a jagged frontier and that hand context engineering on your specific tasks extends your frontier beyond the default, so it is not simply thrown away when a model improves.
cards.evidence_detail: Whiteboard in radial coordinates with illustrative 90%/40%/50% figures, not measured.
cards.landing: Justifies investing in harness tuning even though models improve; counterweight to 'bitter lesson' objections.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: when it wants to send money, that's a permission escalation
cards.claim: Dex says a human-in-the-loop approval of an agent action is not deterministic (the agent could click or fill differently) and proposes per-action signed tokens (Rich Authorization Requests style) that bind exactly the approved action with a short expiry, with read access granted separately from write.
cards.evidence_detail: Design proposal using JWT/passkey signing; no implementation shown.
cards.landing: Closes the gap between 'approved' and 'done': a machine-checkable binding between what the owner approved and what ran; loosely relevant to phase routine compliance checks.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: skills only work if you have a bash tool.
cards.claim: Dex notes skills offload auth and execution to CLIs/curl and so need a bash tool; in locked-down enterprise settings without bash they degrade to prompt modules, and bash trades determinism for flexibility and context efficiency.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoned trade-off, no measurements.
cards.landing: Skills design: each skill should wrap a repo script or CLI (deterministic part) with a prompt shell, not carry logic only in prose.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Do not outsource the thinking. If you let the model make decisions
cards.claim: Dex's rule: do not outsource the thinking; ask the model for options and decide yourself, because a model told to do a thing follows its first tokens down one path while one asked to choose reads what you want.
cards.evidence_detail: Explained during Vaibhav's live design session; Vaibhav adds that models are sycophantic and a suggestion must be marked as a suggestion.
cards.landing: Phase routine: design/decision step should present options for the owner rather than direct instructions; wording rule for prompts that suggest.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: so that you can do brain surgery on it before
cards.claim: Dex says the markdown docs (research, design) exist so the model dumps its thinking and patterns for you to re-steer at a high level before dropping to code.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes RPI use in Riptide; no numbers.
cards.landing: Decisions journal in the draft PR: surface the model's plan in readable form before implementation.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I always want to be able to resume from the document.
cards.claim: Dex keeps every decision tracked in a document outside the context window (unidirectional: read doc, tell Claude, Claude updates doc) so a session can die or drift and be resumed from the doc.
cards.evidence_detail: Contrasted with Vaibhav, who keeps long context and writes to disk only at checkpoints, saying per-decision writes halve his speed.
cards.landing: Directly the P1 cold-resume trial and one-phase-per-session; also the knowledge store: state lives in repo files not chat.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I usually try to recontinue it at over like a hundred K tokens.
cards.claim: Dex's own habit is to restart a session once past about 100K tokens, though he says the dumb-zone figure is a rule of thumb for people without intuition and some reasoning-heavy tasks should stay under 50K while others tolerate 800K.
cards.evidence_detail: Numbers 100K, 50K and 800K are practitioner habits, not measurements; Vaibhav reports 3-4 features at up to 800K with good outcomes.
cards.landing: Context budget rule for phase sessions: a numeric trigger (about 100K) for ending a session and resuming from the PR/decisions journal.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're totally fine at 120 or 220 or 320k tokens
cards.claim: Dex passes on Chris's distinction that long context is fine for reading and summarising documents but multi-turn tool-calling loops (run test, fix, rerun) are where the model spins out.
cards.evidence_detail: Second-hand from a Twitter post; no numbers beyond the quoted token counts.
cards.landing: Verifier/implementer sessions with test loops should be kept short; reading/research sessions can run longer.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: might be going back to Opus 4-5 for certain things
cards.claim: Dex says HumanLayer published early findings on 1M-context models and may go back to Opus 4.5 for some work, and that a 1M window is the same model stretched with techniques like YaRN rather than added intelligence.
cards.evidence_detail: Brief remark; refers to a Kyle blog post and defers the discussion; the YaRN claim is stated as fact without evidence.
cards.landing: Model routing: evidence that a newer or larger-context model is not automatically better for all phases.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: get the foundation there, make it work end to end
cards.claim: Dex endorses building the most foundational layer first and making it work end to end (vertical slices, tracer bullets) instead of making the model design everything up front.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside in the BAML design session.
cards.landing: Phase ordering in the 40-phase plan: thin end-to-end slice before breadth.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: remove that section, and then it'll come up in the design discussion
cards.claim: Dex's tip: delete sections of a ticket you are unsure about so they do not enter as pre-banked decisions; the model then researches code patterns and raises them in the design discussion.
cards.evidence_detail: His own habit; Vaibhav replies his case is novel so no patterns exist.
cards.landing: Plan authoring: mark unknowns as open questions for the design step rather than writing guesses into the plan.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 200 lines of spec that's gonna turn into thousands of lines of code
cards.claim: Dex stresses that one wrong line in a 200-line spec multiplies into thousands of lines of code, which is why hours go into reading the ticket and design before any implementation.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav adds a 12-minute ticket read and about 2.5 hours design plus 5 hours ticket-2 work, then a 16,000-line closures PR done in about 36 hours with sleep; single-developer anecdote.
cards.landing: Owner review of plan before implementation; supports review budget placed on the spec rather than the diff.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: But if it's 30 % wrong, then I know it's easy to just start over
cards.claim: Dex's rule: if an implementation is about 5% wrong, steer it; if about 30% wrong, drop the ticket in again and restart, because tokens are cheap compared to the effort of re-steering a model that has gone down a bad path.
cards.evidence_detail: Endorses Vaibhav's habit of nuking the branch, fixing the ticket and rerunning; percentages are intuition.
cards.landing: Phase routine: an explicit restart rule (discard branch, amend plan, re-run) instead of long repair chains in one session.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it will find a bunch of like bad patterns or bad architecture
cards.claim: Dex says models are sycophantic judges: asked whether code is good they say yes, asked what is wrong they find problems, so a free-form model verdict cannot deterministically evaluate quality.
cards.evidence_detail: Observation from his own posting; no measurement in this episode.
cards.landing: Refuter design: refute-by-default framing is the deliberate counter; also a caution on any verifier that returns an open-ended opinion.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you do a bunch of Boolean classifiers on the thing you're evaluating
cards.claim: Dex's fix for unreliable model grading is to have the model answer many yes/no questions (is it X, does it do Y) and compute the score from those flags in deterministic code.
cards.evidence_detail: Refers to a JP Morgan emails episode from months earlier; no numbers.
cards.landing: Verifier output format: per-register-id boolean checks (fail-before/pass-after) tallied by a script rather than a prose verdict.

cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: you're adding slop at the final layer
cards.claim: Dex and Vaibhav agree that an auto-reviewer (CodeRabbit, 50 comments on a 25,000-line change) adds slop at the final layer because a model always finds something to say; read it and choose, do not pass it all back.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's wording; Dex adds the model's incentive to generate more tokens; Vaibhav has Claude summarise the comments.
cards.landing: Reviewer scope: cap reviewer findings and require the owner to triage; supports capped outputs and against automatic apply of all review comments.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can paralyze two hard tasks at a time.
cards.claim: Dex limits himself to one primary task plus one or two secondary tasks, always returning to the primary when unblocked, to minimise cycle time per task rather than spreading attention.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice; grounded in factory flow theory, no measurement.
cards.landing: Owner workflow: one phase in flight with at most a secondary phase, matches one-phase-per-session.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: optimize a station that is not the bottleneck, the less efficient the overall system becomes
cards.claim: Dex (citing The Goal) argues that optimising non-bottleneck steps adds work in progress and lowers throughput; finish work nearest done first and optimise the slowest step of the pipeline.
cards.evidence_detail: Book summary and a story from an early-career manager; no software data.
cards.landing: Where to spend effort in the harness: find the real bottleneck (owner review? verifier cost?) before tuning a step; relevant to the xhigh-everywhere verifier question.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: be very explicit about when is this, you know, relevant to your task
cards.claim: Dex wraps CLAUDE.md rules in an XML 'important: if you are doing X' block stating exactly when they apply, because the system message tells Claude to ignore context unless highly relevant; his CLAUDE.md is a repo map plus exact commands like the DB query.
cards.evidence_detail: Shows the snippet and a multi-repo template (git pull the branch before research); no adherence numbers.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim and rewrite: make each retained rule conditional on a named situation; map-of-repo style; a pre-research sync step as a routine item.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: this is a deep link into the Riptide app
cards.claim: HumanLayer's PRs carry a link to the artifacts list and a deep link to the task that produced them, so a reviewer can open the agent sessions behind the change.
cards.evidence_detail: Shown on screen with a Closures PR; Dex says no one will read every session.
cards.landing: Draft PR body 'Plan @ sha' plus evidence folder: a link from PR to the session transcript/evidence gives an outside check on whether the routine ran.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have to unlock it by doing 100 sessions or something.
cards.claim: Dex says HumanLayer considered letting experienced users auto-advance past the design discussion but gated it behind many sessions; for now the design step needs human reading, as Vaibhav insists he must know it is correct.
cards.evidence_detail: Half-joking product idea; the human-read design gate is Vaibhav's stated practice.
cards.landing: Phase routine: keep the human checkpoint on design/plan, auto-advance the rest; earn automation by track record.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the benefit is that you get research without opinions.
cards.claim: Dex defends the RPI research step as a separate pass with a context window that stays objective (research questions first, then research), accepting multiple passes over the same code and slower research.
cards.evidence_detail: Brief comment while research ran 15+ minutes; he adds fast code-search models and LSP/call-graph tools as ways to speed it up.
cards.landing: Call-graph/LSP tooling (a skipped item) and research-first agent design: re-opens call-graph tooling.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: auto research doesn't work well unless you have a good way to collect metrics
cards.claim: Dex says auto-research style loops (an agent tuning prompts, models and sub-agents) need a good metric signal, and HumanLayer is building evals on coding agents, e.g. to make the research step faster.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav suggests a latency metric over scenarios of long/short tickets and different codebases; nothing built or measured yet.
cards.landing: Measurement pipeline (explicitly skipped by harness review): marks a re-opening; a metric is the precondition for tuning effort levels.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: automate the process of building confidence that something is stable enough to ship
cards.claim: Dex defines the purpose of testing as automating confidence that a change is stable enough to ship and better than what existed, and with non-deterministic systems wants many sliceable dimensions per test case to see which category moved.
cards.evidence_detail: Restatement of Vaibhav's scenario/metric design (80% scenario thresholds, quorum runners); no data.
cards.landing: Acceptance gate design: scenario-sliced pass rates rather than a single boolean for model-involved behaviour.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: distill them out into another like high level, almost like PRD style.
cards.claim: After a long design discussion, Dex and Vaibhav have the model rewrite the decisions into a fresh clean ticket as if known on day one, then rerun the pipeline; the second design pass is so clean it needs little thought.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav reports about 2.5 hours design plus 5 hours on ticket 2, then auto-advanced implementation; Dex describes the step.
cards.landing: Phase routine: at a session boundary, regenerate the plan from decisions journal so the next session starts from a single clean source.

gaps: Transcripts are auto-captions without speaker labels beyond Dex/Vaibhav tags; a few passages in the prompt-injection episode (demo code) are garbled and were not carded.
README Whiteboards images for the MCP episode (8 images) were not viewable; only the takeaway text was used.
No video, slides or code (BAML testing PR) examined; numbers such as the 16,000-line closures PR, 36 hours and 800K tokens are Vaibhav's spoken claims.
The OpenAI classifier paper and the claimed sub-10ms distilled guardrail were not verified (Vaibhav could not find the link).
